planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or early fall in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Ostrich Plume is a late-blooming thunbergii hybrid whose drooping plumes open well after most arendsii-type astilbes have finished.

directions: Set crowns in rich, evenly moist soil in partial shade, spacing plants far enough apart to show off their arching habit. Ostrich Plume carries loose, weeping sprays of soft rose-pink flowers on gracefully bowed stems above dark green, deeply cut foliage, a distinctly drooping silhouette that sets thunbergii-type astilbes apart from the stiffer upright plumes of most arendsii hybrids. Its later bloom time extends the astilbe season into midsummer, but the same trait that gives it a looser, more sun-tolerant habit also means it needs steady, uninterrupted moisture to avoid crispy leaf margins during hot spells. In the Gulf South, give it afternoon shade, mulch heavily, and expect it to appreciate irrigation during dry summer stretches more than most other perennials in the bed.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Purple Candles is a chinensis-type astilbe noted for handling sun and dry spells better than most arendsii-hybrid selections.

directions: Grow in humus-rich soil with reliable moisture in partial shade, though established clumps tolerate brief dry spells better than most astilbes once rooted in. Purple Candles sends up tall, narrow, densely packed spikes of dark purplish-red flowers held well above a mound of coarse, deeply incised, bronze-green foliage, with color that gradually softens to lighter purple as each plume ages over its long bloom period. As a chinensis-type selection it spreads more readily by rhizome than arendsii hybrids, gradually forming a broader clump rather than staying in a tight crown. Its improved sun and drought tolerance make it one of the more forgiving astilbes for a Gulf Coast shade border, though it still colors and blooms best with consistent moisture through the heat of summer.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Cattleya bears large plumes of bright orchid pink named for its resemblance to the orchid genus.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, organically rich soil in partial to full shade, and mulch to keep roots cool through summer heat. Cattleya produces tall, upright stems topped with large, feathery panicles of vivid orchid-pink flowers that open above new foliage tinged reddish-bronze before maturing to dark green, giving the plant strong color from both flowers and emerging leaves. It is one of the taller arendsii selections and makes a bold vertical accent toward the back of a shaded border or along a woodland path edge. Because it is listed as reliable into zone 9 by some growers, it is a reasonable astilbe to trial in a Gulf Coast garden provided it gets deep afternoon shade and never dries out during the hottest months.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Betty Bowring is the classic white-flowered brunnera, a break from the blue forget-me-not flowers typical of the species.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, keeping the root zone evenly moist through summer since foliage wilts quickly in dry conditions or hot sun. Betty Bowring bears plain green, rough-textured, heart-shaped leaves without the silver patterning of many newer brunnera cultivars, but is instead grown for its airy sprays of small, pure white flowers in spring, a striking contrast to the sky-blue, forget-me-not-like blooms typical of the species. The bright white flowers stand out well against dark green foliage and pair nicely with other shade-garden whites such as astilbe or Solomon's seal. In the Deep South, give this selection its coolest, shadiest spot and supplemental water during summer heat, since brunnera generally performs best where nights stay relatively cool.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Langtrees is an older English selection with a distinctive ring of silver spots around the leaf edge rather than an overall silvered leaf.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, and keep soil evenly moist through summer since the coarse, heart-shaped leaves wilt and scorch quickly if allowed to dry out. Langtrees, also sold as 'Aluminium Spot', bears green leaves rimmed with an even band of small, metallic silver-gray flecks rather than a fully silvered surface, giving it a subtler, more textured variegation than showier modern cultivars. Loose sprays of small, bright blue, forget-me-not-like flowers rise above the foliage in early spring before the leaves fully expand. As one of the older, more thoroughly garden-tested brunnera selections, it is a reliable and well-documented choice for a shaded border, though like other brunnera it wants a cool, consistently moist site and struggles if pushed into strong sun or drought during a Gulf Coast summer.

common_name: Fireworks Solomon's Seal (Gold-Striped Variegated Solomon's Seal)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Fireworks is a Japanese selection with cream-and-yellow striped leaf margins and red-tinted stems, more vigorous with a few hours of morning sun.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, siting it where a few hours of gentle morning sun can reach the arching stems for best variegation and vigor. Fireworks bears egg-shaped green leaves brightly flecked and streaked with creamy white and yellow along red-tinted stems, with the coloring intensifying into a fuller white-edged margin as the clump matures, and small white bell-shaped flowers dangle beneath the arching stems in spring. It spreads by rhizome into a broad, slowly expanding colony that can reach a yard across within several years, faster and showier than the plain species. Give it consistent moisture and a woodland-style leaf mulch, and expect strong performance through Gulf Coast summers, since Polygonatum in general tolerates zone 9 heat far better than many other variegated shade perennials.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; 'Alba' is the pure white-flowered form of hairy toad lily, sold as an open-pollinated seed strain rather than a single clone.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, and keep the root zone consistently damp with a leaf-litter or bark mulch. This selection produces the same orchid-like, upward-facing flowers as the species but in clean, unspotted white rather than the typical purple-speckled lavender, opening along arching stems from late summer into fall when few other shade perennials are still blooming. Because 'Alba' is propagated from seed rather than a single named clone, expect some variation in vigor and flower size between plants, though all share the same crisp white color. It is one of the more heat-tolerant toad lilies for a Gulf Coast garden, but still needs reliably moist soil and deep shade during peak summer to avoid scorched foliage before the fall flower show.
